topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: For a Class B aeroplane, where does the en route phase begin and end?

options.text: 1 000 ft above departure to 1 500 ft above the destination aerodrome
Top of climb to top of descent
400 ft above departure to 1 000 ft above the destination
1 500 ft after departure to 1 000 ft at destination

explanation: For Class B the en route phase runs from 1 500 ft above the departure aerodrome to 1 000 ft above the destination.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: What en route performance requirement applies to a single-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: After an engine failure, reach a forced landing site
It must have a rate of climb of at least 300 ft/min at its cruise level
After engine failure it must reach an aerodrome
It must hold altitude after engine failure

explanation: In the expected weather and after an engine failure, the aeroplane must be able to reach a place where a safe forced landing can be made.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Which two things decide how far a single-engine aeroplane can glide after an engine failure?

options.text: The temperature and the runway length
The cruise altitude and the descent gradient
The mass and the cruise speed
The fuel on board and the wind

explanation: The glide distance depends on the height above the ground and the descent gradient after the engine fails.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: How is the still-air glide distance found from height and descent gradient?

options.text: Height × gradient ÷ 100
Gradient ÷ height × 100
Height ÷ gradient × 100
Height × gradient

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: A single-engine aeroplane cruises 8 000 ft above the ground with a gross glide gradient of 6%. What is its still-air gross glide distance?

options.text: About 20.2 NM
About 21.9 NM
About 8.1 NM
About 2.2 NM

explanation: 8 000 ÷ 6 × 100 = 133 333 ft ÷ 6 080 ≈ 21.9 NM. Using the net gradient of 6.5% gives 20.2 NM.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: For the forced landing rule, how is the gross descent gradient adjusted?

options.text: It is increased by 0.5%
It is multiplied by 1.5
It is reduced by 0.5%
It is used unchanged

explanation: The assumed en route gradient is the gross descent gradient increased by 0.5%. The result is the net gradient, which gives a shorter, safer glide range.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: The gross glide gradient is 6% from 8 000 ft above the ground. What net glide distance must be used?

options.text: About 2.0 NM
About 21.9 NM
About 23.9 NM
About 20.2 NM

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: How is the forced landing rule shown when planning a route?

options.text: The track must stay below 3 000 ft
The track must stay within 5 NM of an airway
The track stays inside net glide circles
The track must pass over at least one aerodrome every hour of flight

explanation: Circles with the net glide distance as radius are drawn around each safe forced landing area; the planned track must stay inside the circles all the way.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Why can flying higher allow a more direct route for a single-engine aeroplane?

options.text: Higher altitudes have fewer obstacles and less traffic to avoid
The wind is always lighter at altitude
A higher altitude gives larger glide circles
The engine is more reliable at altitude

explanation: A greater height gives a longer glide, so the circles around forced landing sites grow and a straighter track can stay within them.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: What is the highest altitude that may be assumed when showing compliance with the forced landing rule?

options.text: The absolute ceiling
Where the MCP climb rate is 300 ft/min
The service ceiling

explanation: The aeroplane may not be assumed to be flying, with the engine at maximum continuous power, above the altitude at which its rate of climb equals 300 ft/min.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: An aeroplane cruises above the 300 ft/min rate-of-climb altitude. How is the extra height treated for the forced landing rule?

options.text: It may not be counted in the glide range calculation
Half of it may be counted
It must be added to the net gradient as a percentage
It may be counted in full

explanation: The aeroplane may fly higher, but the operator may not use the extra height when calculating the glide range to a safe landing area.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: Why does the net gradient mean the planned glide circles are smaller than the aeroplane could actually achieve?

options.text: It allows for icing on the engine
It allows for a heavier aeroplane
It accounts for a tailwind
It adds a safety margin to the descent performance

explanation: Increasing the gradient by 0.5% assumes worse performance than the gross figure, so the planned range is conservative.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: An endurance graph for a light single gives 7.0 h with no reserve. If 45 minutes reserve is to be kept, what endurance is available for planning?
explanation: 7.0 h − 0.75 h = 6.25 h. Such graphs often show both figures, with and without the reserve.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: What must the pilot do to achieve the range and endurance figures in the manual?

options.text: Fly at the best rate of climb speed
Follow the manual, leaning correctly
Fly at full throttle
Keep the mixture fully rich throughout the cruise

explanation: The published figures assume the manual's technique, especially correct leaning of the mixture.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: What is the difference between a range graph and an endurance graph for a light aeroplane?

options.text: One gives distance flown, the other airborne time
They give the same information in different units
One is for jets, the other for propeller aeroplanes
One includes wind, the other does not

explanation: Both are used in the same way, but a range graph gives distance and an endurance graph gives time.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: A single-engine aeroplane has a net glide range of 18 NM. A safe landing area is 21 NM from part of the planned track. What must happen?

options.text: Nothing, because 21 NM is within the gross glide range
The aeroplane must cruise 500 ft lower
The reserve fuel must be increased
The track must be changed to stay within 18 NM of a site

explanation: At every point on the route a safe forced landing area must lie within the net glide range, so the track must be moved.

topic: 09 Single-engine Class B En Route and Descent
question: From 9 000 ft above the ground with a net glide gradient of 7.5%, how far can a single-engine aeroplane be planned to glide?

options.text: About 19.7 NM
About 12.0 NM
About 1.97 NM
About 22.2 NM

question: A single-engine aeroplane's gross glide gradient is 5%. What net gradient must be used for the forced landing rule?
